label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Kelechi Obi,

Yes, this is an actual letter. On paper. In an envelope. You said a proper letter, not a voice note, so I have gone the full distance and paid for postage. Please respect the effort and read it on the train as promised.

At my birthday, while I was supposed to be receiving attention and enjoying myself, you started complaining about work again. Nine years as a quantity surveyor and every day has apparently become the same spreadsheet. When I said you should come and teach maths, you laughed and told me to put it in writing if I was serious.

Well, I’m serious.

Not serious in the sense that I think you should resign tomorrow, buy sixteen biros and start calling yourself Sir by Christmas. Calm down. I mean serious enough to ask you to come to one open evening and find out whether there is anything in this for you.

It is on Thursday 19 November 2026, at 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I’ll come with you. You don’t have to sign anything, apply for anything or announce a dramatic career change. Just come, listen and ask difficult questions. You are very good at asking difficult questions, usually when somebody is trying to serve you food.

The salaried training route I’m talking about starts in September 2027. It lasts one year and you get paid while you train. Applications open soon, which is why I’m raising it now rather than sending you another casual message you can ignore. Going to the open evening would simply mean that, when you decide whether to apply, you’re making an informed decision instead of dismissing the whole thing because your annoying friend mentioned it over birthday drinks.

And before you decide I’ve just chosen a random profession for you because I happen to work in a school, remember who you are.

You got an A in further maths. In Moremi, you were tutoring half our hostel before exams. People would come to you completely lost, and you would sit there and take them through the questions until they understood. You were patient with people who had left an entire semester’s work until the last possible moment. That alone should qualify you for some sort of national honour.

More importantly, you explained things without making anybody feel stupid for asking. Some of us asked twice. Some of us asked the same question again with different wording, hoping you wouldn’t notice. You noticed, but you kept explaining anyway.

That is not a small thing. Plenty of people know their subject. Far fewer can stand in front of somebody who is confused, embarrassed and ready to give up, and help them without making the confusion feel like a personal failure. You can do that. You’ve always been able to do it.

Remember helping my nephew with fractions at Christmas? You used portions of jollof rice on plates. No worksheets, no big speech, just rice and patience. He still talks about it. He understood the fractions because you made them visible and familiar, and because you were funny with him instead of behaving like a man delivering a lecture at a conference. I watched you and thought, this man is wasting himself checking other people’s costings.

I know quantity surveying is useful work. I’m not saying your last nine years have counted for nothing, or that buildings should be constructed by vibes. But useful work can still bore you senseless, and from what you keep telling me, your job is no longer asking much of you except that you keep turning up. You have too much curiosity, patience and personality to spend the next twenty-six years mainly moving numbers around somebody else’s spreadsheet.

Meanwhile, my school in Peckham has 1,100 children, and since September we’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups. I’m not telling you that so you can ride in on a white horse and rescue Peckham. Please remove the cape from your mind. I’m telling you because when I say there is room for somebody like you, I don’t mean it as an inspirational slogan. There are actual children, in actual classrooms, who need somebody steady who knows maths and can explain it properly.

Last month, a Year 11 boy called Damola finally understood simultaneous equations. We had been working on them for three weeks. This was not a magical ten-minute transformation; it was three weeks of trying different approaches and him getting frustrated and me trying not to show that I was frustrated too. Then it clicked.

He shouted, “Is that all??” and the whole class clapped.

I cannot fully explain that moment to you without making it sound bigger or smaller than it was. Nothing outside the room changed. He still had the rest of his work to do. I still had books to mark. But for those few seconds, something that had looked impossible to him had become almost insultingly simple, and everybody in the room got to enjoy it with him. That kind of thing does not happen every day. If it did, we would all be insufferable. But it happens, and when it does, you remember exactly why you came back after the difficult days.

Now for the part where I stop making it sound like a film.

Teaching is hard. Properly hard. The marking is endless. Just when you think you’ve found the bottom of the pile, another class produces books. Behaviour some days is wahala. You can prepare a good lesson and still spend half of it dealing with lateness, missing equipment, arguments or somebody deciding that today is the day they cannot possibly sit in their assigned seat. There are meetings, data, parents, planning and plenty of work that has nothing to do with the satisfying business of explaining maths.

When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice during my first term. Not delicate cinematic tears either. I was sitting there wondering why I had thought this was manageable. So no, I’m not hiding that from you or pretending you would be immune because you’re confident and good with people. It gets better, but it does not get better by magic. You learn, you get faster, you stop taking every difficult lesson as evidence that you’re useless, and gradually you find your footing.

The money also needs an honest conversation. There would be a pay drop in the first year. You have real bills and a real life, so that is not a footnote. The salaried route means you are paid while training, but paid while training is not the same as keeping your current salary. You need to look at the figures properly and decide what is workable.

The holidays are real, although planning and marking can eat into them; nobody should imagine it’s months of lying on a beach. The pension is good, and pay increases as you progress. Those things matter, but they don’t cancel out the first-year sacrifice. I wouldn’t respect your judgement if I tried to wave that away.

All I’m asking is that you give the whole thing a fair hearing. Not the fantasy version where grateful children applaud daily, and not the miserable version where you assume you’d be marking exercise books at midnight forever. The actual job, with the actual numbers and an actual route into it.

You are 34, by the way. Not 103. A woman in my department started teaching at 41, so unless she has been ageing backwards without telling us, you are not too old. Your nine years in quantity surveying are not a prison sentence. You wouldn’t be arriving as somebody with nothing behind him. You would be arriving with mathematical ability, professional experience and years of dealing with people, plus the useful ability to remain calm when everybody else is doing too much.

And I haven’t forgotten what you said on your last birthday: “I just want to do something that matters before 40.”

Only you can decide what matters to you. I’m not appointing myself the manager of your purpose in life. But you cannot keep saying that, then complaining that every working day is the same spreadsheet, and then refuse even to spend one evening investigating something you might genuinely be good at. Well, technically you can. You’re an adult. It would just be a bit silly.

So come to Lewisham with me on Thursday 19 November at 6pm. We’ll listen, you can ask every hard question you like, especially about pay, training, workload and what happens when a class simply refuses to cooperate. Afterwards, you can tell me honestly that it isn’t for you, and I’ll accept that. At least then you’ll be rejecting something you’ve actually looked into.

Or you might come away still unsure but interested enough to take the next small step. That would be fine too. Nobody needs a dramatic decision on the night.

I wouldn’t suggest this just because I want a friend nearby or because I enjoy annoying you, although both are bonuses. I’m suggesting it because I know you, I know the job, and I think there is a real chance you would be very good at it. Patients would benefit from your patience too, but unfortunately you’re not a doctor, so children will have to do.

No forms yet. No resignation. No destiny talk. Just one open evening.

And if you reply to this posted letter with a three-minute voice note, I will know you have no respect for due process.

Abeg, just come.

Your friend since Unilag,
